opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it was a genuine watershed moment, and I say that as someone who was, in a sense, on the other side of it at the time. For a long period in computer vision, we had been building systems around hand-designed features — SIFT, HOG, shape contexts, and so on — and then putting a learning machine like an SVM on top. And these approaches had made steady but incremental progress on benchmarks like PASCAL VOC.

Neural networks were not new, of course. LeCun's convolutional networks had worked beautifully on digit recognition back in the late '80s and '90s. But the skepticism in the vision community was whether they would scale to real, cluttered, natural images with thousands of categories. Many of us felt they hadn't been demonstrated convincingly in that regime.

What Alex, Ilya, and Geoff showed in 2012 was that if you combined three things — a large labeled dataset, which ImageNet provided thanks to Fei-Fei Li's efforts; GPU computing, which made training feasible; and some technical refinements like ReLUs and dropout — you got a dramatic jump in performance. Not a one or two percent improvement, but a really large drop in error rate. That kind of gap gets everyone's attention.

Now, I'll be honest: my own reaction was not immediate conversion. ImageNet classification is a particular task — one object, roughly centered. The question I had was, does this transfer to the problems we really care about, like object detection and localization? So my group, with Ross Girshick and others, worked on that, and that led to R-CNN in 2014, where we showed that features learned on ImageNet gave a huge boost on PASCAL detection. That was, for me, the point where I was convinced, and I think for much of the field as well.

So the significance is twofold. Scientifically, it showed that learned representations, given enough data and computation, beat hand-engineered ones — a lesson that has since repeated in speech, in language, everywhere. And sociologically, it shifted the whole community. Within two or three years, essentially everyone in computer vision was using deep learning. I can't think of many paradigm shifts in science that happened that fast.

That said, I'd add one caution. ImageNet's success also led us to lean heavily on supervised learning with massive labeled datasets, and I've always felt that's not how children learn. Babies learn through interaction, through movement, through being embodied in the world. So the next chapter — self-supervised learning, learning from video, learning through action — is where I think a lot of the deeper questions remain.

r001.rationale: The response says the breakthrough came from combining ImageNet’s large labeled dataset, GPU computing, and neural-network techniques, clearly conveying the data, GPUs, and deep learning combination.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I think people sometimes forget that the ideas weren't new in 2012. Convolutional networks go back to Fukushima's Neocognitron in the late seventies, and Yann LeCun had them working on digits by the late eighties and early nineties. Backpropagation was there. So in a sense, intellectually, the pieces were on the table for twenty years. What Alex and Ilya and Geoff did was show that if you took those ideas and scaled them up, with a big enough dataset and GPUs to do the computation, the thing actually worked, and worked dramatically better than anything else.

And I was, I should say, on the other side of this. I was one of the people who had been doing computer vision the "classical" way, with hand-designed features like SIFT and HOG, and then some kind of learning layered on top. In 2011 the best ImageNet entries were all of that flavor. Then in 2012 their network comes in and cuts the error rate by something like ten points. In our field, a gain of one or two points was a good paper. Ten points was not a good paper, it was a different world.

I remember the reaction among vision people was initially a bit of skepticism, maybe some denial. There was a feeling that this is just a trick, or it only works on this particular benchmark. But the thing about science is that the evidence wins. Within a year or so, my own students, Ross Girshick and others, took the same kind of network and showed it worked for object detection too, which was the other big problem we cared about, and that was R-CNN. And after that there was no going back.

So the significance, to me, is twofold. One is simply the empirical result, that learned representations from data beat decades of human feature engineering. The other is more sociological. It's what made the whole field change its mind in about eighteen months, which is remarkably fast for any scientific community. And I think the lesson, which I've had to internalize myself, is that you have to be willing to be wrong, and to let the data tell you when your favorite approach has run its course.

r001.rationale: The response says the team scaled convolutional-network ideas using a large dataset and GPUs, producing dramatically better results.

astra-6.text:
I think its significance was that it changed what the field believed would work. Before that, much of computer vision involved designing features by hand and then training a classifier on top. Alex’s result showed, very convincingly, that you could learn the features as well, provided you had enough data and enough computation.

And it wasn’t a small improvement. The gap was large enough that people had to pay attention and reconsider their approach. The ingredients—neural networks, convolution, learning from examples—had a history. What came together was the ability to make those ideas work at a scale where they decisively outperformed the alternatives.

That was the turning point: learned representations became central to computer vision. It didn’t mean that visual understanding was solved, but it fundamentally changed how we pursued it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sufficient data and computation alongside neural networks, but it does not identify GPUs as part of the combination behind the breakthrough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Alex’s result was a watershed moment for computer vision. It showed that a neural network trained on a large dataset could learn representations that were much more effective than the features we had been designing by hand. And the difference in performance was large enough that the whole community had to pay attention.

But I would distinguish the breakthrough from the idea that everything in it was new. Neural networks and convolutional architectures had a long history. What came together was the data, the computational resources, and the ability to train a sufficiently large model effectively. Alex demonstrated what that combination could do.

For me, the important change was methodological. Instead of separately designing features and then training a classifier, you could learn the representation and the classifier together. That changed the direction of the field. It was an enormous advance, even though recognizing an object in an image is still only one part of understanding the visual world.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the breakthrough to data, neural networks, and computational resources, but does not specifically identify GPUs as part of the combination.
